text: CAMT should be retained for Layer 2 as a direct HBM/advanced-packaging inspection and metrology candidate with recent HBM-manufacturer order evidence.
ONTO should be retained as a process-control and analytics candidate for advanced packaging, HBM, AI/HPC interconnect metrology, and yield-control workflows.
FORM should be retained as an underfollowed wafer-level test/probe-card candidate tied to known-good-die and known-good-stack requirements in HBM and advanced packages.
Separate HBM-stack-specific exposure from broader 2.5D/3D substrate and OSAT exposure; Amkor is useful context but needs verification for direct HBM-linked revenue.

Need a follow-up non-US/global pass for temporary bonding/debonding, underfill, wafer-thinning, hybrid-bonding, and substrate-chemistry suppliers, because the cleanest HBM-stack tool/material names may be Japanese, Korean, Taiwanese, or European rather than US-listed.

KLIC should remain in the Layer 1 universe as a TCB/advanced-packaging equipment hypothesis; survival requires proof that TCB orders are tied to HBM stack or AI accelerator packaging rather than generic advanced packaging.
CAMT has one of the cleaner inspection/metrology mappings to HBM and advanced packaging; next layer should quantify HBM manufacturer order exposure and repeatability.
FORM is a less obvious HBM test-flow candidate; treat probe-card demand as a yield-gate bottleneck and verify memory/HBM mix in disclosures.

VECO is a diversified equipment name with explicit advanced-packaging wet-process orders involving an HBM manufacturer; next layer must separate HBM-stack exposure from broader foundry/OSAT packaging and photonics demand.

This pass found stronger US-listed equipment/test/inspection candidates than US-listed pure-play HBM underfill or temporary bonding/debonding materials suppliers; materials exposure may sit in non-US-listed Japanese/Korean suppliers or inside diversified conglomerates.
ONTO should remain on the HBM stack process watchlist as a relatively direct US-listed inspection/metrology exposure, especially after Dragonfly G5 HBM4 selection evidence.

KLIC is a lower-attention HBM process-equipment candidate because of first HBM system shipment, FTC, vertical wire, and hybrid-bonding exposure; survival depends on follow-on production-order evidence.
CAMT belongs in the inspection/metrology lane for advanced packaging and HBM-related yield control, but needs tighter verification of HBM-specific revenue versus broader advanced-packaging demand.

For this node, separate direct HBM stack-process tools from broader substrate/2.5D/OSAT capacity; Amkor is a reference capacity asset, while ONTO/KLIC/CAMT are closer to process-control or process-tool bottlenecks.

US-listed pure-play materials suppliers for HBM underfill, temporary bonding/debonding chemistry, and ultra-thin wafer handling remain sparse; later passes should search OTC/ADR and Japan/Korea/Taiwan listings separately.
KLIC should be tracked as an underfollowed HBM/advanced-packaging bonding-tool candidate, especially around thermocompression bonding, 2.5D/3D packaging and any HBM-specific system shipments.

CAMT is a strong inspection/metrology candidate for HBM stack and advanced-packaging yield control; verify whether recent HBM manufacturer orders are direct stack-flow exposure or broader packaging inspection.
For this node, separate direct HBM stack-process tools from general substrate/OSAT advanced-packaging exposure; otherwise the universe becomes diluted with generic AI package-capacity names.

Need a follow-up search specifically for US-listed or ADR material suppliers in temporary bonding/debonding adhesives, underfill, TSV chemicals and wafer-thinning consumables; current pass is heavier on tools and OSAT capacity.

MEC Company / MECGF should be carried forward as the most node-pure underfollowed candidate for copper adhesion/surface-treatment chemistry, but US OTC ticker/liquidity and current AI/HPC revenue exposure require verification.
Ajinomoto / AJINY should be carried forward as the ABF film reference asset owner; the key research issue is purity because ABF is embedded in a diversified food and amino-science conglomerate.

Element Solutions / ESI is a US-listed underfollowed hypothesis for IC-substrate wet chemistry, copper plating, copper adhesion, and surface finishes; must verify competitive position versus MEC and revenue materiality.

For FC-BGA / ABF substrates, yield-critical materials and process chemistry may matter more than simple substrate throughput; therefore evidence should prioritize product qualification, customer concentration, defect/yield reduction claims, and pricing power.
US-listed direct exposure is limited because several likely leaders are Japan/Taiwan/Korea-listed or OTC. Later layers should explicitly separate investability/liquidity from bottleneck relevance.

The purest copper-bonding surface-chemistry chokepoint appears to be MEC Company, but this pass did not verify a clean US OTC/ADR ticker; keep 4971.T as a non-US shadow reference rather than a US-listed candidate.
AJNMY is a US-tradable OTC ADR for Ajinomoto and is the main accessible reference candidate for ABF insulating film, but AI exposure is embedded inside a diversified food/materials company.
MKSI is an underfollowed second-order candidate because Atotech supplies package-substrate surface-treatment chemistry and equipment, including ABF/SAP-related processes.

ONTO is an underfollowed yield-control candidate adjacent to FC-BGA/ABF constraints; its direct material exposure is weak, but its inspection/metrology exposure to advanced IC substrates and AI packaging is supported by company disclosures.

For this node, separate material-control points from substrate makers and yield-control tool vendors: Ajinomoto/MEC are the upstream control points; Ibiden/Unimicron are reference substrate makers; MKSI/ONTO are second-order yield and process-enablement plays.

MKSI should remain in the underfollowed lane for ABF/FC-BGA substrate process chemistry because Atotech explicitly targets package substrates, SAP/ABF electroless copper metallization and adhesion/surface-treatment steps.

ESI is a lower-confidence underfollowed candidate: plausible specialty-chemistry exposure through MacDermid Alpha and advanced packaging/IC substrate offerings, but AI/HPC ABF substrate revenue linkage must be verified before promotion.
Ajinomoto remains the primary reference chokepoint for ABF insulating film, but its diversified business mix reduces purity as a US-tradable AI substrate materials asset.

MEC Company appears highly relevant to copper surface-treatment chemistry, but US-tradability and ticker access need verification; keep as a non-US/public-market mapping gap rather than a Layer 1B US-listed candidate for now.
Add AJINY as the reference ABF-film supplier for the FC-BGA / ABF package substrate materials node; not pure-play but structurally central.
Add MECGF as the highest-priority underfollowed discovery candidate for copper-to-resin adhesion and surface-treatment chemistry beneath AI package substrate makers.
Add IBIDY / IBIDF as a reference substrate-maker customer anchor for mapping ABF film and surface-treatment chemistry demand.
Add DD as a broad US-listed second-order advanced packaging and IC substrate materials candidate; exposure is plausible but diluted and needs segment-level verification.

Several strong node candidates are not clean US exchange listings; future passes should verify OTC availability and liquidity for MECGF, JCU, Japan Pure Chemical, Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB, Shinko Electric, and Samsung Electro-Mechanics.

For this node, separate substrate makers from substrate-material suppliers: Ajinomoto and MEC may capture value across substrate-maker winners, while Ibiden/Unimicron carry customer/socket and capacity-cycle risk.

VECO should be carried forward as the highest-priority US-listed underfollowed candidate for the optical_interconnect_epitaxy_tools node because it maps directly to MOCVD/MBE/deposition tools used in photonics and compound semiconductor capacity.

COHR and LITE are reference leaders for AI datacenter optical components, lasers and transceivers; useful as demand anchors, but likely already high-attention and less suitable for the underfollowed lane.

MTSI belongs in the discovery lane despite large-cap size because it is often labeled as analog/RF/telecom/defense semiconductor rather than AI optical infrastructure, while its 1.6T silicon photonics laser and component exposure is direct.

Need a follow-up Layer 1C search for US-listed or ADR wafer/epi substrate names, test/metrology suppliers, packaging/assembly houses, and non-US leaders such as Aixtron to complete the upstream photonics capex map.

VECO should be promoted to the focused underfollowed discovery lane for the optical_interconnect_epitaxy_tools node because it has direct official evidence of InP laser manufacturing equipment orders tied to 800G/1.6T hyperscale optical demand.

AXTI belongs in the materials/substrate watchlist for this node as an InP/GaAs substrate supplier, but later layers must verify revenue mix, capacity, export-control exposure, and whether substrate supply is truly gating AI optical ramps.

AAOI is not a pure upstream equipment/materials name, but its disclosed in-house MBE/MOCVD laser fabrication makes it more relevant to the epitaxy/laser-capacity node than a generic optical-module vendor.

The evidence chain for this node is strongest where company disclosures explicitly connect AI/hyperscale optical bandwidth demand to 800G/1.6T transceivers, InP laser production, and MOCVD/IBD/wet-processing tool orders.
Need a separate non-US/ADR pass for Aixtron, IQE, JX Advanced Metals, and other InP/GaAs wafer, epi, and MOCVD/metrology suppliers; this pass stayed focused on US-listed candidates.

VECO should remain a priority underfollowed candidate for the optical-interconnect epitaxy-tool node because it directly supplies compound semiconductor / photonics process tools and has recent company commentary linking silicon-photonics momentum to AI data-center expansion.

AXTI should remain in the Layer-1 universe as an InP/GaAs substrate hypothesis; survival requires proof that InP revenue is driven by AI datacenter lasers/PICs rather than legacy telecom or 5G cycles.
SMTC is a hidden-dependency candidate after acquiring HieFo; the key check is whether InP optoelectronic device capacity and optical-platform design wins become financially material.
POET fits only as a speculative_shadow candidate: strong thematic mapping to 800G/1.6T optical engines, but needs hard evidence of production revenue, customer pull-through, and manufacturing scale.

Reference anchors LITE and COHR were not included in the four-candidate list to preserve underfollowed focus, but they should be tracked as context for EML/InP laser pricing, customer qualifications, and upstream tool/substrate pull-through.

The falsification path for this node is: if AI optics growth is satisfied mainly by incumbent laser/module capacity without new InP/GaAs epi-tool or substrate capex, then VECO/AXTI exposure should be downgraded versus module vendors.

VECO should remain a priority underfollowed candidate for the optical_interconnect_epitaxy_tools node because it has direct company-disclosed InP laser equipment orders tied to 800G/1.6T hyperscale transceiver manufacturing.

AXTI should be tracked as a substrate-side candidate, but later layers must stress-test export-permit risk, China manufacturing concentration, revenue materiality and whether InP demand is durable beyond a short inventory cycle.
POET belongs in the speculative_shadow lane: named design-win evidence exists, but survival requires proof of volume production, customer purchase commitments and material revenue.

For this node, the most actionable US-listed upstream chain appears to be: hyperscaler AI bandwidth demand -> 800G/1.6T transceivers -> EML/CW lasers and optical engines -> InP substrates and epitaxy -> MOCVD/IBD/wet-process tools.

Aixtron appears highly relevant to MOCVD/compound-semiconductor epitaxy but was not included in the candidate list because this pass prioritized US-listed/common-share accessibility; verify whether US OTC ADR treatment is acceptable for future Serenity universe passes.

Sakai Chemical / SACIF should be tracked as the most node-pure underfollowed public candidate for barium titanate dielectric powders, but OTC liquidity and customer evidence are major Layer 2 gating items.

Vishay / VSH is an accessible US-listed underfollowed MLCC/passive-component hypothesis, but current AI-server exposure evidence is weak and must be verified through product qualification or customer/distributor signals.
Murata / MRAAY remains the primary reference benchmark for AI-server MLCC demand, product mix, and pricing; use it to validate whether the chokepoint is migrating upstream to powder suppliers.

Layer 2 should search Japanese-language primary sources for Sakai's hydrothermal BaTiO3, sub-100nm dielectric-powder capability, MLCC customer qualification, and revenue contribution from electronic dielectric materials.
MRAAY should remain the reference MLCC leader for this node; it is too large/high-attention for the underfollowed lane but necessary for triangulating AI-server MLCC demand.
TYOYY and YAGOY are the most plausible US OTC-accessible underfollowed MLCC/passive-component candidates found in this pass.
VSH is a NYSE-listed speculative shadow candidate: confirmed MLCC product exposure, but AI-server qualification and revenue relevance remain unproven.

The strongest upstream BaTiO3 powder evidence points to Sakai Chemical, Nippon Chemical Industrial, and private Vibrantz/Ferro; clean US-listed exposure to sub-100nm barium titanate powder remains a coverage gap.
Layer 2 should separate MLCC makers from dielectric-powder suppliers and require evidence that AI-server demand is incremental rather than merely a recovery in automotive/consumer MLCC cycles.

SACIF / Sakai Chemical should be carried forward as the highest-purity underfollowed upstream barium-titanate powder candidate, but only as a hypothesis until primary disclosures confirm electronic-materials revenue mix, AI-server MLCC demand linkage, and customer qualification.

VSH / Vishay is a US-listed mid-cap second-order passive-components candidate for AI-server MLCC/power-system screening; current evidence supports MLCC product capability but not direct AI-server chokepoint exposure.

TDK and Murata should remain reference anchors for the node because both have explicit server/data-center or AI-server MLCC evidence; they should not crowd out upstream powder suppliers in later underfollowed passes.

Need a dedicated non-US/OTC mapping pass for Sakai Chemical, Nippon Chemical Industrial, Fuji Titanium/Kyoritsu, Yageo/KEMET, Walsin, Holy Stone, and Kyocera AVX to separate true high-end AI-server MLCC exposure from automotive/consumer MLCC cyclicality.

US-listed pure-play exposure to high-end sub-100nm barium titanate powder for MLCCs appears weak. The most relevant upstream names found in this pass are Japan-listed or private, so US candidates should be treated as downstream/adjacent unless direct sourcing or design-win evidence emerges.

VSH is the strongest US-exchange underfollowed candidate for this node because it has official high-voltage MLCC products and a mid-cap profile, but AI-server revenue/design-win evidence remains unverified.

KN is a speculative shadow candidate: it has specialty MLCC/high-voltage capacitor capability, but current public evidence points more to defense, industrial, medtech, optical networks, telecom, and automotive than AI-server MLCC demand.

Murata and TDK should be retained as reference leaders for AI-server MLCC product requirements, while Sakai Chemical and TODA KOGYO should be tracked as non-US upstream powder comparables for the true dielectric-material bottleneck.

POWL is a high-relevance electrical distribution and switchgear candidate for the AI data-center electrical balance-of-system node; direct evidence exists, but the market cap and attention level have risen, so treat as underfollowed only relative to mega-cap AI infrastructure leaders.

NVT is a direct electrical-products candidate due to enclosures, switchgear, bus systems, intelligent PDUs and modular electrical-equipment enclosure exposure; verify data-center revenue mix and Avail/Trachte contribution.
IESC is a strong project-execution/labor-capacity candidate because SEC filings explicitly tie strong demand to data centers and flag labor/capacity as a constraint.

Need a follow-up search for smaller USD 300M-10B names below the now-rerated POWL/IESC/NVT tier, especially transformer components, relays, busbar fabricators, enclosure makers, electrical subcontractors, and interconnection/permitting consultants.

POWL should be retained as a high-priority underfollowed electrical-equipment candidate for AI data-center power distribution because company disclosures explicitly connect AI/data-center development with medium-voltage switchgear opportunities and backlog growth.

IESC should be retained as a project-execution chokepoint candidate; next layer must verify the percentage of backlog/revenue tied to data centers and whether margins are sustainable as labor and scheduling constraints rise.
NVT should be tracked despite larger market cap because the Avail acquisition provides direct switchgear, bus systems, enclosures, and control-building exposure to data centers and utilities.
ATKR is a weaker but plausible second-order candidate; evidence currently supports data-center end-market participation but not yet a clear AI-specific backlog or pricing-power thesis.

For this node, backlog/order evidence and lead-time commentary are more important than generic data-center exposure; future passes should penalize companies that only list data centers as one of many end markets without project-specific demand signals.

Need a follow-up search for US-listed transformer-specific suppliers, power-relay/protection vendors, electrical distributors, and permitting/interconnection consultants; this pass primarily surfaced switchgear, bus systems, raceway, and electrical contracting.
POWL is the cleanest direct underfollowed electrical-BOS candidate found in this pass because it explicitly ties AI/data-center demand to medium-voltage switchgear opportunities and backlog.
IESC maps to the project-execution bottleneck: electrical and technology system installation plus custom engineered infrastructure solutions for data centers.
ATKR should be tracked as a second-order cable-management/conduit/cable-tray supplier; evidence is product-level and needs revenue-materiality verification.
AZZ is a speculative shadow candidate: electrical and infrastructure exposure is clear, but the AI data-center linkage needs stronger evidence through orders, customer mix, or management commentary.

For later Serenity layers, prioritize backlog quality, lead times, customer concentration, fixed-price contract risk, labor availability, and data-center revenue mix over generic AI narrative language.
POWL should remain in the Layer 1B underfollowed lane for data-center electrical balance-of-system because it has direct fiscal 2026 evidence of a >$400 million data-center order and record backlog.

IESC should remain in the Layer 1B underfollowed lane as a project-execution and custom engineered solutions candidate; Q2 fiscal 2026 Infrastructure Solutions growth was explicitly tied primarily to data-center demand.

ATKR is a speculative shadow candidate: it has plausible exposure through electrical products for data-center infrastructure, but direct AI/data-center revenue contribution and chokepoint status need verification before promotion.

Need a focused follow-up search for busbar, enclosure, protection relay, transformer subcomponent, and modular power-distribution suppliers that are US-listed or have liquid ADRs; current pass found stronger evidence for switchgear/OEM and contractor lanes than for subcomponents.

Electrical balance-of-system should be tracked as a combined hardware-plus-execution chokepoint: switchgear/transformers are only one side; qualified electrical labor, modular construction, field services and interconnection execution may be equally limiting.
Keep VRT as the high-attention reference anchor for data-center liquid-cooling/CDU exposure, but do not let it crowd out component and supplier-layer discovery.

NVT and MOD are direct liquid-cooling infrastructure candidates with stronger public product evidence than most generic industrial names, but both now exceed the preferred USD 300M-10B hunting band and require market-pricing checks.

INV is a small-cap speculative-shadow candidate because Accelsius gives unusually direct two-phase direct-to-chip cooling exposure; survival in later layers requires proof of commercialization, ownership economics, and field reliability.
The node appears to split into at least four investable subnodes: CDU/rack fluid distribution, heat rejection/chillers, two-phase direct-to-chip systems, and leak/reliability monitoring.

Need a separate supplier-component pass for valves, pumps, quick disconnects, sensors, coolants, filtration, and leak-detection companies; many may be private, non-US-listed, or buried inside diversified industrials.
MOD should remain in the AI liquid-cooling component universe because its SEC filing explicitly identifies CDUs and immersion solutions for high-density data-center computing.
NVT should remain in the underfollowed lane because it has explicit CDU, manifold, rear-door heat-exchanger and rack-level liquid-cooling product exposure, but revenue materiality needs verification.
WTS is a speculative-shadow candidate for valves, flow-control and leak/water-management components in data-center liquid-cooling loops; do not upgrade until design-in or revenue evidence is found.

Need a follow-up pass on non-US or OTC component specialists in leak detection, valves, pumps, quick disconnects, dielectric coolants, and cold plates; many apparent pure plays are private or foreign-listed.

SPXC and other heat-rejection/cooling-tower names may belong in an adjacent facility heat-rejection node rather than this rack/CDU/cold-plate component node unless direct liquid-cooling evidence improves.
MOD should remain in the thermal-management liquid-cooling universe because company filings explicitly connect AI/HPC heat loads to demand for hybrid and liquid cooling.
NVT is a hidden CDU/enclosure candidate; the next filter should verify revenue materiality and AI-rack design wins rather than relying only on product existence.
INV/Accelsius is a speculative small-cap route into two-phase direct-to-chip cooling; survival depends on confirming Innventure's economic ownership and shareholder look-through exposure.
ECL/CoolIT, TT/LiquidStack and VRT/Intel validate the node as strategically important, but they are better treated as context anchors than the main underfollowed discovery lane.

Need a separate component-level pass for pumps, valves, leak detection, coolant chemistry, sensors, and third-party reliability testing; many likely suppliers are private, foreign-listed, or buried in broad industrial portfolios.

MOD should remain on the thermal-management node list as a direct data-center cooling name with official AI/data-center order evidence, but it has re-rated into large-cap territory and should not crowd out smaller component names in later passes.

NVT is a high-quality reference-lane name for CDUs, manifolds, controls, services, and OCP/AI rack liquid-cooling architecture; include as context even though market cap is above the ideal underfollowed range.

WTS enters the speculative_shadow lane as a leak-detection, water-management, flow-control, and liquid/chilled-water systems candidate; survival requires proof that data centers are material and tied to AI liquid-cooling buildouts.

BMI enters the speculative_shadow lane as a flow-measurement and water-quality monitoring candidate for data-center cooling loops; survival requires evidence of design-ins with CDU vendors, mechanical contractors, hyperscalers, or colo operators.

The thermal/liquid-cooling node should be split in later layers into: system integrators, CDU/manifold/rack modules, cold plates and quick disconnects, pumps/valves/flow meters, coolant chemistry/water treatment, leak detection, and field-service/commissioning.

Private companies appear important in cold plates and liquid-cooling modules; later public-market mapping should explicitly check whether public substitutes have real exposure or whether the chokepoint is mostly private/captive.

Separate the AI accelerator supply chain into HBM stack flow and package-substrate flow. HBM stack flow has cleaner direct exposure to HBM unit growth; package substrate flow is tied to accelerator package count and complexity.

High-priority AI bottleneck nodes for Layer 2A: HBM stack process tools/yield, advanced packaging capacity, FC-BGA/ABF substrate yield, ABF insulating film, copper-to-resin surface chemistry, data-center power distribution, liquid cooling, optical interconnect upstream materials/tools, and ultra-high-purity quartz.
ABF film and copper-adhesion chemistry appear to be low-attention upstream process-material chokepoints because value can accrue regardless of which substrate maker wins share.
AI capex should be tracked as full-stack procurement: foundry, advanced packaging, memory, power delivery, rack manufacturing, and geographic redundancy rather than only accelerator purchase orders.
HBM generation transitions and denser AI packages should be monitored for evidence of increased demand for bonding, thinning, inspection, metrology, probe-card, underfill, and test suppliers.
Grid interconnection delays, transformer availability, behind-the-meter power deals, and liquid-cooling qualification wins are likely catalysts for the AI physical-infrastructure layer.

Need primary-source verification for concentration claims around ABF film and copper-adhesion chemistry, including company filings, customer qualification evidence, segment revenue, and capacity expansion disclosures.

Need primary-source filings and earnings-call checks for suppliers in inspection, metrology, probe cards, bonding tools, switchgear, liquid cooling, and compound-semiconductor substrates before any company-level prioritization.
Need to verify which catalysts are already priced by market attention and valuation before moving from industry-chain map to security-level funnel layers.

VECO should be tracked as an underfollowed upstream optical-interconnect capacity supplier: not a transceiver name, but a compound-semiconductor deposition/equipment candidate tied to InP laser capacity and AI datacenter bandwidth growth.

POWL should be tracked as an underfollowed AI data-center electrical balance-of-system candidate, with the key gating evidence being whether large data-center orders become repeatable backlog rather than one-off project revenue.
CAMT maps most cleanly to advanced-packaging and HBM inspection/metrology; next layer should verify HBM-specific order repeatability and tool-of-record status.
KLIC remains a hypothesis-stage HBM bonding and advanced assembly candidate because the company must prove that initial HBM system shipments become production-scale repeat orders.

MECGF/MEC Company is a potentially high-quality but access-friction underfollowed candidate in copper-to-resin package-substrate chemistry; verify ticker validity, liquidity, segment contribution, and competitive share before escalation.
ONTO is a one-layer-away yield-enabler for advanced IC substrates and advanced packaging; monitor whether AI chiplet substrate ramps are material to orders and not just broad semi recovery.

FORM should be tracked as a known-good-die/known-good-stack test hardware candidate for HBM and 2.5D/3D packaging, but current relationship is still hypothesis-stage pending HBM-specific probe-card evidence.

NVT belongs in the reference lane for AI data-center cooling and electrical connection/protection; the core evidence gap is whether liquid-cooling/CDU/manifold exposure is large enough to move consolidated results.
AJINY/Ajinomoto is a reference-lane ABF film chokepoint with strong node-level evidence but weak purity as an equity vehicle because exposure is embedded inside a diversified conglomerate.
All candidate relationships require primary-source verification from company filings, earnings transcripts, investor presentations, and segment disclosures before Layer 2C prioritization.
Need current market-cap, liquidity, analyst-coverage, and valuation-pricing checks to distinguish underfollowed chokepoints from already-discovered AI infrastructure beneficiaries.
Need separation of direct AI revenue, indirect semiconductor-cycle recovery, and generic industrial demand for each candidate to avoid overstating AI purity.

VRT should remain a reference leader for AI data-center power and thermal infrastructure, not an underfollowed discovery candidate. Use it to calibrate backlog, margins, liquid-cooling mix and field-service economics for smaller suppliers.

MKSI maps to the AI substrate-yield branch through Atotech chemistry, metallization, plating, laser-processing and process-control exposure. Key survival test is whether company disclosures show meaningful Electronics & Packaging growth tied to IC substrates and advanced packaging.

AAOI maps to the AI optical interconnect branch as an underfollowed-to-repriced vertical-integration candidate. Key survival tests are 800G/1.6T shipment ramp, laser-fab yield, gross margin and customer concentration.

IESC maps to the electrical execution and labor-capacity chokepoint rather than the manufactured equipment layer. Evidence must separate data-center backlog and margin from generic electrical contracting growth.
MOD maps to AI data-center thermal management, but the chokepoint claim depends on whether growth is in liquid-cooling/CDU-like systems or broader HVAC/chiller demand.

COHR and LITE are reference optical leaders for 800G/1.6T, lasers and photonic components. Use them to trace demand pull into upstream compound-semiconductor substrates, epitaxy tools, optical testing and photonic packaging candidates.

MRAAY and TTDKY are reference names for AI-server MLCC and passive-component power-delivery exposure. Underfollowed alpha, if any, may sit one layer lower in barium titanate powder, electrode materials, high-end MLCC equipment or niche power-delivery component suppliers.
Need current market-cap and analyst-coverage checks for all underfollowed-lane tickers because several names in the chunk may have already repriced above the intended USD 300M-10B hunting band.

Need primary-source verification for each ticker's direct AI exposure: filings, investor presentations, earnings calls, segment revenue, backlog, customer concentration, capex, product qualification and margin commentary.

Need falsification plan by node: if backlog growth is broad data-center or cyclical recovery rather than AI-density-driven scarcity, downgrade the chokepoint relationship; if margins compress during volume growth, downgrade pricing-power claims.
IBIDY / IBIDF should remain a reference-anchor ticker for AI package-substrate demand, not the primary underfollowed alpha target; use it to validate upstream material and chemistry suppliers.
ESI is a plausible underfollowed AI substrate-chemistry mapping, but survival to later layers requires primary evidence of share at ABF/FC-BGA substrate makers and materiality to electronics revenue.
ATKR is a second-order AI data-center electrical BOS hypothesis; verify whether data centers are a measurable business driver rather than generic nonresidential construction exposure.
YAGOY, TYOYY, and VSH form a passive-component subcluster for AI-server MLCC and power-delivery content; current evidence is mostly adjacency and needs board-level qualification or revenue-mix proof.
POET and INV are speculative_shadow names where partnership headlines are insufficient; require production revenue, repeat orders, qualification status, and reliability/yield evidence.

SMTC may deserve an underfollowed optical-interconnect bridge slot because it can connect signal-integrity ICs and optical component exposure, but HieFo materiality and customer adoption must be verified.
Need primary-source filings and investor decks for each ticker in this chunk; current Layer 2B mapping relies heavily on external theme-level evidence and candidate-provided hypotheses.
Need current market-cap, analyst-coverage, and valuation/pricing checks before ranking underfollowed status; several names may already be discovered or too broad to isolate AI exposure.
Need customer concentration and qualification-cycle evidence for substrate chemistry, MLCCs, optical engines, and cooling systems because chokepoint value depends on difficulty of substitution.
BMI should remain in the speculative_shadow lane for AI thermal-management instrumentation until company-level filings or product/customer evidence prove data-center or liquid-cooling loop exposure.
DD maps to adjacent advanced-packaging materials rather than the proven ABF film or copper-to-resin chokepoint; avoid treating DD as a direct Ajinomoto/MEC substitute without qualification evidence.
SPXC maps to facility-side data-center heat rejection and cooling infrastructure; the key survival test is whether AI/data-center backlog or revenue is material and disclosed.
KN is the weakest candidate in this chunk and should be downgraded unless direct AI-server, optical-module, PSU, accelerator-board, or high-voltage rack-power capacitor design-in evidence is found.

Layer 2B lacks primary-source company evidence for BMI, DD, SPXC, and KN. Next layer should search filings, investor decks, earnings transcripts, product/application notes, and customer case studies before ranking.

Need current market-cap, analyst-coverage, valuation, and revenue-mix checks for the chunk to determine whether these are truly underfollowed AI bottleneck candidates or already priced industrial compounders.
